blocks.body:
At a party of six people, some pairs know each other and some do not. However the acquaintances are arranged, there are always three people who all know each other or three who are mutual strangers. With five people this can fail. Ramsey theory is the study of statements of this shape: once a structure is large enough, any way of splitting it into a few classes leaves one class containing a large orderly piece.

The basic object is a colouring of the edges of a complete graph, and the basic question is quantitative: how many vertices force a one-coloured complete subgraph of a given size? The answer, the Ramsey number, is known exactly only for a handful of small cases, and its growth rate is one of the central open problems of combinatorics.

blocks.title: The party problem
blocks.body:
Translate the party into a graph: six vertices, every pair joined by an edge, the edge red if the two people know each other and blue otherwise. This is a 2-colouring of the edges of the complete graph $K_6$ (see [[graph-basics]]). We want a monochromatic triangle: three vertices whose three connecting edges have the same colour.

Pick any vertex $v$. It has five edges, so by [[pigeonhole]] at least three of them share a colour, say red, going to $a$, $b$, $c$. If any of the edges $ab$, $bc$, $ca$ is red, it forms a red triangle with $v$. If none is red, then $abc$ is a blue triangle. Either way we are done.

Five vertices are not enough. Place them at the corners of a regular pentagon, colour the five sides red and the five diagonals blue. The red edges form a 5-cycle, which has no triangle, and the blue edges form another 5-cycle (the pentagram), which has no triangle either.

So six is the exact threshold. The general question asks the same thing with triangles replaced by larger complete graphs, and with possibly different targets for the two colours.

blocks.title: Ramsey number
blocks.body:
For integers $k, \ell \ge 1$, the Ramsey number $R(k,\ell)$ is the least $n$ such that every colouring of the edges of $K_n$ in red and blue contains a red $K_k$ or a blue $K_\ell$. The diagonal case is written $R(k) = R(k,k)$.

Equivalently, thinking of the red edges as a graph $G$: every graph on $R(k,\ell)$ vertices contains a clique of size $k$ or an independent set of size $\ell$, and some graph on $R(k,\ell)-1$ vertices contains neither. The party problem says $R(3,3) = 6$.

blocks.title: Why the numbers exist
blocks.body:
It is not obvious that $R(k,\ell)$ is finite: perhaps for some $k$ there are arbitrarily large colourings with no monochromatic $K_k$. The argument for triangles generalises, and it gives a recursive bound.

Small cases first. A single vertex is a $K_1$ of either colour, so $R(1,\ell) = R(k,1) = 1$. For $R(2,\ell)$: if any edge is red we have a red $K_2$; otherwise everything is blue, so $\ell$ vertices suffice and $\ell - 1$ do not (colour all edges blue). Hence $R(2,\ell) = \ell$, and by symmetry $R(k,2) = k$. Swapping the colours shows $R(k,\ell) = R(\ell,k)$ in general.

blocks.title: Ramsey's theorem with the Erdős–Szekeres bound
blocks.body:
For all $k, \ell \ge 2$,
$$R(k,\ell) \le R(k-1,\ell) + R(k,\ell-1).$$
Consequently $R(k,\ell)$ is finite for all $k,\ell \ge 1$ and
$$R(k,\ell) \le \binom{k+\ell-2}{k-1}, \qquad\text{in particular}\qquad R(k) \le \binom{2k-2}{k-1} < 4^{k}.$$

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
Assume $R(k-1,\ell)$ and $R(k,\ell-1)$ are finite, and let $n = R(k-1,\ell) + R(k,\ell-1)$. Take any red/blue colouring of $K_n$ and a vertex $v$. The other $n-1$ vertices split into the set $A$ of those joined to $v$ by a red edge and the set $B$ of those joined by a blue edge. Since $|A| + |B| = n - 1$, we cannot have both $|A| \le R(k-1,\ell) - 1$ and $|B| \le R(k,\ell-1) - 1$, because then $|A|+|B| \le n-2$. So one of the following holds.

1. $|A| \ge R(k-1,\ell)$. Inside $A$ there is a red $K_{k-1}$ or a blue $K_\ell$. A blue $K_\ell$ finishes the proof; a red $K_{k-1}$ together with $v$ is a red $K_k$, since all edges from $v$ to $A$ are red.
2. $|B| \ge R(k,\ell-1)$. Inside $B$ there is a red $K_k$, which finishes the proof, or a blue $K_{\ell-1}$, which together with $v$ is a blue $K_\ell$.

This proves the recursive inequality, and finiteness follows by induction on $k+\ell$ from the base cases $R(1,\ell) = R(k,1) = 1$.

For the binomial bound, also induct on $k+\ell$. The bound holds when $k=1$ or $\ell=1$, because $\binom{\ell-1}{0} = \binom{k-1}{k-1} = 1$. For $k,\ell \ge 2$, the recursion and the induction hypothesis give
$$R(k,\ell) \le \binom{k+\ell-3}{k-2} + \binom{k+\ell-3}{k-1} = \binom{k+\ell-2}{k-1}$$
by Pascal's rule. Finally $\binom{2k-2}{k-1}$ is one term of $\sum_j \binom{2k-2}{j} = 4^{k-1}$, so it is less than $4^k$.

blocks.title: Small values and the growth of R(k)
blocks.body:
The recursion gives $R(3,3) \le R(2,3) + R(3,2) = 6$, which is exact. Exact values are known only for a few small pairs. Three facts worth knowing:

- $R(3,4) = 9$ (see the second example below).
- $R(4,4) = 18$, proved by Greenwood and Gleason in 1955. The lower bound comes from the Paley graph on 17 vertices: join $i$ and $j$ in $\mathbb{Z}/17$ when $i - j$ is a nonzero square modulo 17. This graph has no clique and no independent set of size 4.
- $R(5,5)$ is unknown. It is known that $43 \le R(5,5) \le 46$; the upper bound came from a large computer-assisted argument in 2024.

For general $k$ the two bounds are exponential with different bases. The upper bound above is essentially $4^k$. In 1947 Erdős proved $R(k) > 2^{k/2}$ for all $k \ge 3$ by showing that a uniformly random colouring of $K_n$ with $n = \lfloor 2^{k/2} \rfloor$ has, with positive probability, no monochromatic $K_k$. This argument is the subject of [[probabilistic-method]]. Together:
$$2^{k/2} < R(k) \le 4^{k} \qquad (k \ge 3).$$
(The inequality $\sqrt{2}^{\,k} \le R(k)$ also holds for $k = 2$, where $R(2) = 2$, but not for $k = 1$, where $R(1) = 1$.)

Since 1947 the base $\sqrt2$ in the lower bound has not been improved, only constant factors in front. For the upper bound, Conlon (2009) improved $\binom{2k-2}{k-1}$ by a factor that grows faster than any power of $k$, but the base 4 stood until 2023, when Campos, Griffiths, Morris and Sahasrabudhe proved
$$R(k) \le (4-\varepsilon)^k$$
for a fixed $\varepsilon > 0$ and all large $k$. This was the first exponential improvement over the 1935 bound of Erdős and Szekeres. Whether $\lim R(k)^{1/k}$ exists, and what it is, remains open.

A striking feature of the lower bound is that it is not constructive. Random colourings work, but nobody knows an explicit colouring of $K_n$ whose largest monochromatic clique is as small as a random one's, of order $\log n$.

blocks.title: More colours and larger subsets
blocks.body:
The same argument works with $r$ colours. Let $R_r(k)$ be the least $n$ such that every $r$-colouring of the edges of $K_n$ contains a monochromatic $K_k$. To see that $R_r(k)$ is finite, merge colours $2, \dots, r$ into one: by the two-colour theorem, any $r$-colouring of $K_n$ with $n = R\big(k, R_{r-1}(k)\big)$ has a $K_k$ in colour 1 or a complete subgraph on $R_{r-1}(k)$ vertices that uses only colours $2, \dots, r$, and by induction on $r$ the latter contains a monochromatic $K_k$. For triangles with three colours the answer is $R_3(3) = 17$, also due to Greenwood and Gleason. Their lower-bound colouring of $K_{16}$ uses the field with 16 elements: colour the edge $\{x,y\}$ according to which coset of the subgroup of cubes contains $x - y$.

Edges are 2-element subsets. Ramsey's original 1930 theorem, proved as a lemma in a paper on decision problems in logic, colours $m$-element subsets.

blocks.title: Ramsey's theorem (finite form)
blocks.body: For all positive integers $m$, $r$ and $k$ there is an $N$ such that, however the $m$-element subsets of an $N$-element set are coloured with $r$ colours, there is a $k$-element subset all of whose $m$-element subsets have the same colour.

blocks.title: The general philosophy
blocks.body:
The proof of the general theorem is an induction on $m$, using the case $m - 1$ in the way that the graph case used the case of single vertices. Its bounds grow like towers of exponentials, and for $m \ge 3$ the true growth is still not understood (see [[hypergraphs]]).

The theorem is one of several results with the same structure: colour a large object, find a structured monochromatic piece. Schur's theorem (monochromatic solutions of $x + y = z$) follows directly from the graph case, as the third example shows. Van der Waerden's theorem on monochromatic arithmetic progressions needs a different proof (see [[ramsey-arithmetic]]). The infinite version, that every colouring of the pairs of an infinite set has an infinite monochromatic subset, is the starting point of [[infinite-combinatorics]].

blocks.title: At least two monochromatic triangles
blocks.body: Show that every red/blue colouring of the edges of $K_6$ contains at least two monochromatic triangles.
blocks.solution:
Call a pair of edges at a common vertex a bichromatic angle if the two edges have different colours. If vertex $v$ has $r_v$ red edges and $5 - r_v$ blue edges, it is the apex of $r_v(5 - r_v)$ bichromatic angles. Since $r_v \in \{0,\dots,5\}$, this is at most $2 \cdot 3 = 6$.

A monochromatic triangle has no bichromatic angles. A triangle that is not monochromatic has two edges of one colour and one of the other, so exactly two of its three angles are bichromatic. Every bichromatic angle lies in exactly one triangle, the one obtained by closing it up. Hence
$$2 \cdot \#\{\text{non-monochromatic triangles}\} = \sum_v r_v(5 - r_v) \le 6 \cdot 6 = 36.$$
So at most 18 of the $\binom{6}{3} = 20$ triangles are non-monochromatic, and at least 2 are monochromatic.

The bound is sharp. Split the six vertices into two groups of three, colour edges inside a group red and edges between the groups blue. The two groups are red triangles; there is no blue triangle, since the blue graph is bipartite.

blocks.title: Computing R(3,4)
blocks.body: Prove that $R(3,4) = 9$.
blocks.solution:
The recursion gives $R(3,4) \le R(2,4) + R(3,3) = 4 + 6 = 10$. We improve this by one using parity.

Suppose the edges of $K_9$ are coloured with no red triangle and no blue $K_4$. Fix a vertex $v$, let $A$ be its red neighbours and $B$ its blue neighbours, so $|A| + |B| = 8$.

- Inside $A$ there is no red edge, since such an edge together with $v$ would be a red triangle. So $A$ spans only blue edges, and as there is no blue $K_4$, $|A| \le 3$.
- Inside $B$ there is no blue triangle, since with $v$ it would give a blue $K_4$. There is also no red triangle. As $R(3,3) = 6$, $|B| \le 5$.

Since $|A| + |B| = 8$, both bounds are attained: every vertex has exactly 3 red edges. Then the red graph has $9 \cdot 3 / 2$ edges, which is not an integer. This contradiction shows $R(3,4) \le 9$.

For the lower bound, colour $K_8$ on vertices $\mathbb{Z}/8$ by making $\{i,j\}$ red when $i - j \equiv \pm 1$ or $4 \pmod 8$. A red triangle would need three differences from $\{\pm1, 4\}$ that add up to $0 \pmod 8$, and no such combination exists. Checking the 70 four-element subsets (or arguing by hand) shows that each contains a red edge, so there is no blue $K_4$. Hence $R(3,4) > 8$.

blocks.title: Schur's theorem from Ramsey's theorem
blocks.body: Show that for every $r$ there is an $N$ such that, however $\{1, 2, \dots, N\}$ is coloured with $r$ colours, there are $x, y, z$ of the same colour with $x + y = z$ ($x = y$ is allowed). For $r = 2$, find the least such $N$.
blocks.solution:
Let $N = R_r(3) - 1$ and fix a colouring $\chi$ of $\{1,\dots,N\}$. Colour the edges of the complete graph on vertices $\{0, 1, \dots, N\}$ by giving the edge $\{i, j\}$ the colour $\chi(|i - j|)$. This graph has $R_r(3)$ vertices, so it has a monochromatic triangle $a < b < c$. Put $x = b - a$, $y = c - b$, $z = c - a$. These three numbers lie in $\{1,\dots,N\}$, have the same colour, and satisfy $x + y = z$.

For two colours this gives $N = R(3,3) - 1 = 5$. It is the least possible: colour $1$ and $4$ red, $2$ and $3$ blue. The red sums $1+1$, $1+4$, $4+4$ equal $2$, $5$, $8$, none red; the blue sums $2+2$, $2+3$, $3+3$ equal $4$, $5$, $6$, none blue. So four numbers can be coloured with no monochromatic solution, while five cannot.

blocks.body:
- A monochromatic $K_k$ means all $\binom{k}{2}$ edges among the $k$ chosen vertices have one colour. It is not enough for the edges along a path or a cycle through them to agree.
- $R(k,\ell)$ is a threshold for every colouring. To prove $R(k,\ell) > n$ you must exhibit one colouring of $K_n$ (or prove one exists); to prove $R(k,\ell) \le n$ you must handle all colourings.
- The binomial bound is not exact in general: it gives $R(4,4) \le 20$, while the truth is 18.
- The lower bound $R(k) > 2^{k/2}$ says that a good colouring exists, without telling you how to build one. The explicit constructions known are much weaker.
- Ramsey's theorem finds a monochromatic substructure, not a large colour class. Questions about how many edges force a $K_k$, whatever their colour, belong to Turán's theorem (see [[extremal-graphs]]), which has quite different answers.

- [[probabilistic-method]]: Erdős's lower bound for $R(k)$ is the founding example of proving existence by random choice.
- [[ramsey-arithmetic]]: Schur, van der Waerden and Rado colour integers instead of edges and look for monochromatic solutions of equations or arithmetic progressions.
- [[infinite-combinatorics]]: the infinite Ramsey theorem and the arrow notation for cardinals, where some questions turn out to be independent of the usual axioms of set theory.
- [[hypergraphs]]: Ramsey numbers for colourings of triples and larger sets grow much faster and are far less understood.
- [[discrete-geometry]]: the Erdős–Szekeres theorem on convex polygons in point sets can be derived from Ramsey's theorem for 4-element subsets.
- [[extremal-graphs]] and [[graph-coloring]] study related forcing questions where density, not colouring, is the hypothesis.

1. Use the recursion to show $R(3,5) \le 14$.
2. Prove that $R_3(3) \le 17$: every 3-colouring of the edges of $K_{17}$ has a monochromatic triangle.
3. Show that for $k, \ell \ge 2$, if $R(k-1,\ell)$ and $R(k,\ell-1)$ are both even, then $R(k,\ell) \le R(k-1,\ell) + R(k,\ell-1) - 1$.
4. Prove that every 2-colouring of the edges of $K_7$ contains at least four monochromatic triangles, by adapting the angle-counting argument for $K_6$.

blocks.body:
Suppose you want to show that some object exists: a colouring with no large monochromatic clique, a tournament where every pair of players is beaten by a third, a large subset of integers with no solution to $x + y = z$. Building one explicitly can be very hard. The probabilistic method takes another route: choose an object at random and show that it has the property with positive probability. Then at least one object has it.

On a finite set of objects this is only counting in another language: "probability positive" means "the number of good objects is not zero". The language matters because probability supplies tools, above all linearity of expectation, that make the counting easy.

blocks.title: The first example: Ramsey numbers
blocks.body:
Recall from [[ramsey]] that $R(k)$ is the least $n$ such that every red/blue colouring of the edges of $K_n$ has a monochromatic $K_k$. To prove $R(k) > n$ we need one colouring of $K_n$ with no monochromatic $K_k$.

Colour each edge of $K_n$ red or blue independently with probability $\tfrac12$ each. A fixed set $S$ of $k$ vertices spans $\binom{k}{2}$ edges. They are all red with probability $2^{-\binom k2}$ and all blue with the same probability, so $S$ is monochromatic with probability $2^{1-\binom k2}$. There are $\binom nk$ sets $S$, and the probability that at least one of several events happens is at most the sum of their probabilities (the union bound). This gives the inequality Erdős used in 1947.

blocks.title: Erdős's lower bound for Ramsey numbers
blocks.body:
If
$$\Pr\big[\text{some } K_k \text{ monochromatic}\big] \le \binom nk 2^{1-\binom k2} < 1,$$
then $R(k) > n$. In particular $R(k) > 2^{k/2}$ for every $k \ge 3$.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
The first statement was shown above: if the union bound is less than 1, then with positive probability no $k$-set is monochromatic, so at least one colouring of $K_n$ has no monochromatic $K_k$.

For the second, let $k \ge 3$ and $n = \lfloor 2^{k/2} \rfloor$. Using $\binom nk \le n^k / k!$ and $n^k \le 2^{k^2/2}$,
$$\binom nk 2^{1-\binom k2} \le \frac{2^{k^2/2}}{k!}\, 2^{1 - \frac{k^2}{2} + \frac{k}{2}} = \frac{2^{1 + k/2}}{k!}.$$
For $k = 3$ this is $2^{2.5}/6 < 5.66/6 < 1$. Going from $k$ to $k+1$ multiplies the numerator by $\sqrt 2$ and the denominator by $k + 1 \ge 4$, so the quantity stays below 1 for all $k \ge 3$. Hence $R(k) > n = \lfloor 2^{k/2} \rfloor$, and since $R(k)$ is an integer, $R(k) \ge \lfloor 2^{k/2}\rfloor + 1 > 2^{k/2}$.

blocks.title: Expectation and linearity
blocks.body: The union bound is the crudest tool. The workhorse is the following observation about any random variable $X$ on a finite probability space (see [[random-variables]]): $X$ cannot always be smaller than its average.

blocks.title: First-moment principle
blocks.body: Let $X$ be a random variable on a finite probability space. If $\mathbb E[X] \ge t$, then $\Pr[X \ge t] > 0$. Likewise, if $\mathbb E[X] \le t$, then $\Pr[X \le t] > 0$.

Let the outcomes be $\omega_1, \dots, \omega_N$ with probabilities $p_i > 0$ summing to 1. If $X(\omega_i) < t$ for every $i$, then $\mathbb E[X] = \sum p_i X(\omega_i) < \sum p_i t = t$, contradicting $\mathbb E[X] \ge t$. The second statement is the same argument with the inequalities reversed.

blocks.title: How the principle is used
blocks.body:
To use the principle we need $\mathbb E[X]$, and that is where linearity of expectation comes in: if $X = X_1 + \dots + X_m$, then $\mathbb E[X] = \mathbb E[X_1] + \dots + \mathbb E[X_m]$, whether or not the $X_i$ are independent. Typically $X$ counts something and $X_i$ is the indicator of the $i$-th possible occurrence, so $\mathbb E[X_i]$ is just a probability.

A first illustration. In a tournament every pair of $n$ players plays once and there are no draws; draw an arrow from winner to loser. A Hamiltonian path is an ordering $v_1, \dots, v_n$ of all the players in which each $v_i$ beat $v_{i+1}$. Choose the result of each game by a fair coin. For each of the $n!$ orderings, the $n - 1$ required results occur with probability $2^{-(n-1)}$. By linearity the expected number of Hamiltonian paths is $n!/2^{n-1}$, so some tournament on $n$ players has at least that many. Szele observed this in 1943, before Erdős's Ramsey paper; it was the paper of 1947 that made the method widely known.

blocks.title: Alterations: choose at random, then repair
blocks.body:
Sometimes a random object is almost good, and a few local fixes finish the job. The expected number of fixes then enters the calculation.

Let $G$ be a graph with $n$ vertices and $m \ge n/2$ edges. Put each vertex into a set $S$ independently with probability $p$. Then $\mathbb E|S| = pn$, and the expected number of edges with both ends in $S$ is $p^2 m$. Now delete one endpoint of each such edge. What remains is an independent set (no two of its vertices are adjacent) of size at least $|S| - e(S)$, whose expectation is $pn - p^2 m$. Choosing $p = n/(2m)$, which is at most 1, gives
$$\mathbb E\big[|S| - e(S)\big] = \frac{n^2}{2m} - \frac{n^2}{4m} = \frac{n^2}{4m},$$
so $G$ has an independent set of at least $n^2/(4m)$ vertices. In terms of the average degree $d = 2m/n$ this reads $n/(2d)$.

The same trick improves the Ramsey bound: delete one vertex from each monochromatic $K_k$ of a random colouring. This shows $R(k) > n - \binom nk 2^{1-\binom k2}$ for every $n$. Optimising over $n$, the plain union bound gives $R(k) > (1+o(1))\frac{1}{e\sqrt2}\,k\,2^{k/2}$ and the alteration bound gives $R(k) > (1+o(1))\frac{1}{e}\,k\,2^{k/2}$, so the gain is a constant factor $\sqrt2$.

blocks.title: Rare, nearly independent events: the local lemma
blocks.body:
The union bound needs the bad events' probabilities to add up to less than 1. If there are very many bad events, each unlikely, this fails even when most pairs of events have nothing to do with each other. If all bad events were independent, the probability that none occurs would be the product of the probabilities $1 - \Pr[A_i]$, which is positive. The Lovász local lemma (Erdős and Lovász, 1975) interpolates between these extremes. Its symmetric form reads as follows.

Let $A_1, \dots, A_N$ be events such that each $A_i$ has probability at most $p$, and each $A_i$ is mutually independent of the collection of all other $A_j$ except at most $d$ of them. If $e\,p\,(d+1) \le 1$, then with positive probability none of the $A_i$ occurs.

We state it without proof (Alon and Spencer give a two-page proof). Notice that the number of events $N$ does not appear. Applied to Ramsey numbers, it gives $R(k) > (1 + o(1)) \frac{\sqrt2}{e}\, k\, 2^{k/2}$, a result of Spencer. The base $\sqrt2$ has never been improved.

The fourth main tool is concentration: a sum of many independent small random variables is very likely close to its mean. A typical bound: if $X$ is the sum of $n$ independent random signs $\pm1$, then $\Pr[|X| \ge \lambda] \le 2e^{-\lambda^2/(2n)}$. A subset with $s \le n$ points obeys the same bound with $s$ in place of $n$, which is only stronger. Combined with the union bound, this shows that for any $n$ subsets of an $n$-element set there is a red/blue colouring of the points in which every subset has $|\#\text{red} - \#\text{blue}| < \sqrt{2n\ln(4n)}$: the failure probability is at most $n \cdot 2e^{-\ln(4n)} = \tfrac12$. This is the starting point of [[discrepancy]] theory.

blocks.title: Large bipartite subgraphs
blocks.body: Show that every graph with $m$ edges contains a bipartite subgraph with at least $m/2$ edges.
blocks.solution: Put each vertex on the left or right side independently with probability $\tfrac12$. An edge is cut (its ends on opposite sides) with probability $\tfrac12$, so by linearity the expected number of cut edges is $m/2$. By the first-moment principle some partition cuts at least $m/2$ edges, and the cut edges form a bipartite subgraph.

blocks.title: Tournaments where every pair is beaten
blocks.body: Say a tournament has property $S_k$ if for every set of $k$ players there is another player who beat all of them. Show that a tournament with property $S_k$ exists whenever $\binom nk (1 - 2^{-k})^{n-k} < 1$. For $k = 2$, how large an $n$ does this give, and can you do better?
blocks.solution:
Take a random tournament on $n$ players. For a fixed set $K$ of $k$ players and a fixed outsider $v$, the probability that $v$ beat all of $K$ is $2^{-k}$. Different outsiders involve disjoint sets of games, so the probability that no outsider beat all of $K$ is $(1 - 2^{-k})^{n-k}$. By the union bound over the $\binom nk$ choices of $K$, the probability that property $S_k$ fails is at most $\binom nk (1-2^{-k})^{n-k}$. If this is less than 1, some tournament has property $S_k$.

For $k = 2$ the condition $\binom n2 (3/4)^{n-2} < 1$ first holds at $n = 21$. The random method is not sharp here. On the players $0, 1, \dots, 6$, let $i$ beat $j$ when $i - j$ is one of the nonzero squares modulo 7, which are $1, 2, 4$. Exactly one of $i - j$ and $j - i$ is a square (because $-1 \equiv 6$ is not a square mod 7), so this is a tournament. Checking the 21 pairs shows that every pair is beaten by some third player: for instance $\{0, 1\}$ is beaten by $2$, since $2 - 0 = 2$ and $2 - 1 = 1$ are squares. So 7 players suffice for $S_2$.

blocks.title: Independent sets from a random order (Caro–Wei)
blocks.body: Let $G$ be a graph with vertex degrees $d(v)$. Prove that $G$ has an independent set of size at least $\sum_v \frac{1}{d(v) + 1}$.
blocks.solution:
Order the vertices uniformly at random, and let $I$ be the set of vertices that come before all of their neighbours in the order. Two adjacent vertices cannot both be in $I$, since one of them comes first, so $I$ is independent.

A vertex $v$ is in $I$ exactly when it is first among the $d(v) + 1$ vertices consisting of $v$ and its neighbours. Each of these is equally likely to come first, so $\Pr[v \in I] = 1/(d(v)+1)$. By linearity $\mathbb E|I| = \sum_v 1/(d(v)+1)$, and by the first-moment principle some ordering gives an independent set at least this large.

For the 5-cycle the bound is $5/3$, so there is an independent set of size 2; for the Petersen graph (10 vertices, all of degree 3) it is $5/2$, so there is one of size 3 (the true maximum is 4). By convexity of $x \mapsto 1/(x+1)$, the bound is at least $n/(d + 1)$ where $d$ is the average degree, which is Turán's theorem in complementary form (see [[extremal-graphs]]).

blocks.title: Sum-free subsets
blocks.body: A set of integers is sum-free if it contains no $x, y, z$ (with $x = y$ allowed) such that $x + y = z$. Prove that every set $A$ of $n$ nonzero integers contains a sum-free subset with more than $n/3$ elements.
blocks.solution:
Choose a prime $p = 3k + 2$ larger than $|a|$ for every $a \in A$; there are infinitely many primes of the form $3k + 2$ (an elementary proof imitates Euclid's argument with the number $3N - 1$). Then no element of $A$ is divisible by $p$.

Let $C = \{k+1, k+2, \dots, 2k+1\}$, viewed as residues modulo $p$. The set $C$ is sum-free modulo $p$: the sum of two elements of $C$ lies between $2k+2$ and $4k+2$, and modulo $p = 3k + 2$ these numbers are the residues $2k+2, \dots, 3k+1$, then $0$, then $1, \dots, k$, none of which is in $C$.

Now pick $x$ uniformly from $\{1, 2, \dots, p-1\}$. For each fixed $a \in A$, the map $x \mapsto xa \bmod p$ is a bijection of the nonzero residues, so $xa \bmod p$ is uniform on them and lands in $C$ with probability
$$\frac{|C|}{p - 1} = \frac{k+1}{3k+1} > \frac13.$$
By linearity, the expected number of $a \in A$ with $xa \bmod p \in C$ is greater than $n/3$, so some $x$ gives a subset $B \subseteq A$ with $|B| > n/3$ and $xB \bmod p \subseteq C$.

$B$ is sum-free: if $a + b = c$ with $a, b, c \in B$, then $xa + xb \equiv xc \pmod p$ with all three residues in $C$, which is impossible.

blocks.body:
- The first-moment principle gives $\Pr[X \ge \mathbb E X] > 0$, not $\Pr[X > \mathbb E X] > 0$. If $X$ is constant there is nothing above the mean.
- Linearity of expectation needs no independence, but computing a probability like "no outsider beats all of $K$" as a product does. Check independence each time you multiply.
- The union bound is an inequality. Showing that the sum of probabilities is large proves nothing about whether a bad event must happen.
- A positive probability can be astronomically small. The method proves existence; it does not by itself give an efficient way to find the object, though in many cases random choice is practical: in the bipartite-subgraph example a random partition cuts at least $m/2$ edges with probability at least $1/(m+1)$, by Markov's inequality applied to the number of uncut edges.
- In the local lemma the condition is about mutual independence from all but $d$ events, which is stronger than pairwise independence.

- [[ramsey]]: the 1947 lower bound $R(k) > 2^{k/2}$ is still the best up to constant factors.
- [[extremal-graphs]] and [[graph-coloring]]: Erdős used random graphs with an alteration step to show there are graphs with no short cycles and arbitrarily large chromatic number.
- [[hypergraphs]] and [[set-systems]]: random colourings bound the number of edges needed to prevent a 2-colouring (property B), and random permutations give short proofs of Sperner-type inequalities.
- [[discrepancy]]: concentration inequalities and the union bound give the first estimates for how evenly a colouring can split a family of sets.
- [[sidon-sets]] and [[additive-combinatorics]]: random sets with alterations give lower bounds for many extremal problems on integers.
- [[limit-theorems]]: concentration bounds are quantitative forms of the law of large numbers, and [[primality]] testing is a classic randomized algorithm.

blocks.body:
A club with $n$ members wants to form committees. How many committees can it have if no committee may be a subset of another? How many if every two committees must share a member? How many committees of exactly $k$ people, all pairwise sharing a member? Questions like these, about the largest family of subsets of an $n$-element set subject to a rule, make up extremal set theory.

The answers are often clean binomial coefficients, and the proofs are short double-counting arguments that are worth knowing by heart: they recur throughout combinatorics, coding theory and theoretical computer science.

blocks.title: Notation and first observations
blocks.body:
Write $[n] = \{1, 2, \dots, n\}$. A family $\mathcal F$ is a set of subsets of $[n]$. The family of all subsets has $2^n$ members, and the family $\binom{[n]}{k}$ of all $k$-element subsets has $\binom nk$ members (see [[counting]]).

Two rules dominate the subject.

1. No member contains another. The family $\binom{[n]}{k}$ obeys this rule, because distinct sets of the same size cannot contain each other. The best single layer is the middle one, $k = \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$, since the binomial coefficients increase up to the middle and then decrease.
2. Every two members intersect. The family of all sets containing the element 1 obeys this rule and has $2^{n-1}$ members. Among $k$-element sets, all $k$-sets containing 1 form an intersecting family of size $\binom{n-1}{k-1}$, called a star.

The theorems below say that, under the right conditions, these simple families are the best possible.

blocks.title: Antichain, intersecting family
blocks.body:
A family $\mathcal F$ of subsets of $[n]$ is an antichain (or Sperner family) if there are no distinct $A, B \in \mathcal F$ with $A \subset B$. It is intersecting if $A \cap B \neq \emptyset$ for all $A, B \in \mathcal F$.

An antichain is a family with no comparable pair; an intersecting family is one with no disjoint pair.

blocks.title: Sperner's theorem and the LYM inequality
blocks.body:
If $\mathcal F$ is an antichain of subsets of $[n]$, then
$$\sum_{A \in \mathcal F} \frac{1}{\binom{n}{|A|}} \le 1 \qquad\text{(LYM inequality)},$$
and consequently
$$|\mathcal F| \le \binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor} \qquad\text{(Sperner, 1928)}.$$

blocks.title: Proof by counting chains
blocks.body:
A maximal chain is a sequence $\emptyset = C_0 \subset C_1 \subset \dots \subset C_n = [n]$ with $|C_i| = i$. Choosing such a chain is the same as choosing the order in which the elements $1, \dots, n$ are added, so there are $n!$ maximal chains.

Fix a set $A$ with $|A| = a$. A maximal chain passes through $A$ exactly when the first $a$ elements added are those of $A$; there are $a!$ orders for them and $(n-a)!$ for the rest, so $a!(n-a)!$ maximal chains pass through $A$.

No maximal chain passes through two members of an antichain, since any two sets on one chain are comparable. Counting pairs (chain, member of $\mathcal F$ on that chain) therefore gives
$$\sum_{A \in \mathcal F} |A|!\,(n-|A|)! \le n!.$$
Dividing by $n!$ gives the LYM inequality. Since $\binom{n}{|A|} \le \binom{n}{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor}$ for every $A$, each term of the sum is at least $1/\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$, so $|\mathcal F| / \binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor} \le 1$.

blocks.title: Intersecting families of k-sets
blocks.body:
For families of arbitrary sets, the intersecting condition is easy: a family cannot contain both a set and its complement, and the $2^n$ subsets fall into $2^{n-1}$ complementary pairs, so an intersecting family has at most $2^{n-1}$ members, as many as a star.

For $k$-element sets the question is harder, and there is a threshold. If $n < 2k$, any two $k$-subsets of $[n]$ intersect, so all $\binom nk$ of them form an intersecting family, which is larger than a star whenever $k < n$. If $n \ge 2k$, the star wins.

blocks.title: Erdős–Ko–Rado theorem
blocks.body:
Let $n \ge 2k$. If $\mathcal F$ is an intersecting family of $k$-element subsets of $[n]$, then
$$|\mathcal F| \le \binom{n-1}{k-1}.$$
For $n > 2k$, equality holds only for stars.

blocks.title: Katona's cycle proof of the bound
blocks.body:
Place the elements of $[n]$ around a circle in some order $\sigma$. An arc is a set of $k$ elements that are consecutive around the circle; there are $n$ arcs.

Claim: an intersecting family contains at most $k$ of the $n$ arcs of $\sigma$. Suppose it contains some arc $A$, occupying positions $i, i+1, \dots, i+k-1$ (indices modulo $n$). Any other arc meeting $A$ either starts at one of the positions $i+1, \dots, i+k-1$ or ends at one of the positions $i, \dots, i+k-2$. Pair, for $j = 1, \dots, k-1$, the arc ending at position $i+j-1$ with the arc starting at position $i+j$. Together these two arcs cover the $2k$ consecutive positions from $i+j-k$ to $i+j+k-1$, and since $n \ge 2k$ these positions are distinct, so the two arcs are disjoint. The family contains at most one arc from each pair, so at most $1 + (k-1) = k$ arcs in total.

Now count pairs $(\sigma, A)$ with $\sigma$ a circular order (up to rotation, there are $(n-1)!$) and $A \in \mathcal F$ an arc of $\sigma$. By the claim there are at most $k\,(n-1)!$ such pairs. On the other hand, a fixed $k$-set $A$ is an arc of exactly $k!\,(n-k)!$ circular orders: glue $A$ into one block, arrange the block and the other $n - k$ elements around the circle in $(n-k)!$ ways, and order $A$ inside the block in $k!$ ways. Hence
$$|\mathcal F| \cdot k!\,(n-k)! \le k\,(n-1)!, \qquad |\mathcal F| \le \frac{k\,(n-1)!}{k!\,(n-k)!} = \binom{n-1}{k-1}.$$
(The uniqueness statement for $n > 2k$ needs a closer look at the case of equality and is omitted here.)

blocks.title: Sunflowers
blocks.body: Sperner and Erdős–Ko–Rado bound the size of families that avoid a pattern. The sunflower lemma goes the other way: every large family contains a pattern. A sunflower with $p$ petals is a collection of $p$ sets $S_1, \dots, S_p$ whose pairwise intersections are all equal to the same set $Y$, the core. Removing the core leaves $p$ disjoint petals $S_i \setminus Y$. The core may be empty, in which case a sunflower is just $p$ pairwise disjoint sets.

blocks.title: Sunflower lemma (Erdős–Rado, 1960)
blocks.body: Let $k, p \ge 1$. Every family of more than $k!\,(p-1)^k$ distinct sets, each of size $k$, contains a sunflower with $p$ petals.

Induction on $k$. For $k = 1$ the sets are distinct singletons; more than $p - 1$ of them gives $p$ pairwise disjoint ones, a sunflower with empty core.

For $k \ge 2$, let $\mathcal F$ have more than $k!\,(p-1)^k$ members and choose a maximal subfamily $\mathcal D \subseteq \mathcal F$ of pairwise disjoint sets. If $|\mathcal D| \ge p$, any $p$ of its sets form a sunflower. Otherwise the union $U$ of the sets in $\mathcal D$ has at most $(p-1)k$ elements, and by maximality every member of $\mathcal F$ meets $U$. By [[pigeonhole]] some element $x \in U$ lies in more than
$$\frac{k!\,(p-1)^k}{(p-1)k} = (k-1)!\,(p-1)^{k-1}$$
members of $\mathcal F$. Removing $x$ from these members gives that many distinct sets of size $k - 1$, which by induction contain a sunflower $S_1 \setminus\{x\}, \dots, S_p\setminus\{x\}$. Putting $x$ back into every set keeps all pairwise intersections equal (each gains $x$), so $S_1, \dots, S_p$ is a sunflower in $\mathcal F$.

blocks.title: How good is the sunflower bound?
blocks.body: Take $k$ disjoint blocks of $p - 1$ elements each, and let the family consist of all sets that pick one element from each block. It has $(p-1)^k$ members and contains no sunflower with $p$ petals, so the truth lies between $(p-1)^k$ and $k!\,(p-1)^k$. Erdős and Rado conjectured that $C_p^k$ sets suffice for a constant $C_p$ depending only on $p$; this sunflower conjecture is still open. A breakthrough of Alweiss, Lovett, Wu and Zhang (2019), with later refinements by others, lowered the bound to the form $(C p \log k)^k$ for an absolute constant $C$, well below $k!$.

blocks.title: Divisors that do not divide each other
blocks.body: What is the largest set of divisors of $30030 = 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdot 7 \cdot 11 \cdot 13$ such that no member divides another?
blocks.solution: Because $30030$ is a product of six distinct primes, each divisor corresponds to the set of primes dividing it, and $d \mid d'$ exactly when the set for $d$ is contained in the set for $d'$. So we want the largest antichain of subsets of a 6-element set, which by Sperner's theorem has $\binom63 = 20$ members. The divisors that are products of exactly three of the six primes achieve it.

blocks.title: The threshold in Erdős–Ko–Rado
blocks.body: Find the largest intersecting family of 2-element subsets of $[5]$, and of 3-element subsets of $[5]$. Compare with $\binom{n-1}{k-1}$.
blocks.solution:
For $k = 2$, $n = 5 \ge 2k$. Think of 2-sets as edges of a graph on 5 vertices; intersecting means any two edges share a vertex. Such a graph is a star (all edges through one vertex) or a triangle. A star has at most 4 edges and a triangle has 3, so the maximum is $4 = \binom41$, as the theorem says. The triangle $\{12, 13, 23\}$ is a maximal intersecting family that is not a star, but it is smaller.

For $k = 3$, $n = 5 < 2k$. Any two 3-subsets of $[5]$ meet, because together they would otherwise need 6 elements. So all $\binom53 = 10$ of them form an intersecting family, larger than $\binom42 = 6$. The hypothesis $n \ge 2k$ cannot be dropped.

blocks.title: Signed sums in a short interval
blocks.body: Let $a_1, \dots, a_n$ be real numbers with $|a_i| \ge 1$ for all $i$. Among the $2^n$ sums $\varepsilon_1 a_1 + \dots + \varepsilon_n a_n$ with $\varepsilon_i \in \{+1, -1\}$, show that at most $\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$ lie in any open interval of length 2.
blocks.solution:
Replacing $a_i$ by $-a_i$ only relabels the sums (swap the sign $\varepsilon_i$), so we may assume $a_i \ge 1$ for all $i$. For a subset $S \subseteq [n]$ let
$$s(S) = \sum_{i \in S} a_i - \sum_{i \notin S} a_i,$$
the sum with $\varepsilon_i = +1$ exactly for $i \in S$. If $S \subsetneq T$, then
$$s(T) - s(S) = 2\sum_{i \in T \setminus S} a_i \ge 2,$$
so $s(S)$ and $s(T)$ cannot both lie in an open interval of length 2. Hence the sets $S$ whose sums lie in a given such interval form an antichain, and Sperner's theorem bounds their number by $\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$.

The bound is sharp: with all $a_i = 1$, the sum is $2|S| - n$, and the $\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$ sets of size $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ all give the same sum. This is Erdős's 1945 solution of the Littlewood–Offord problem, which asks how concentrated random signed sums can be.

blocks.body:
- Sperner's theorem allows sets of different sizes, so it is not enough to observe that the middle layer is the largest layer. The proof has to rule out cleverly mixed families, which is why the LYM inequality weights each set by $1/\binom{n}{|A|}$ instead of simply counting.
- Erdős–Ko–Rado needs $n \ge 2k$. For $n < 2k$ every family of $k$-sets is intersecting.
- For $n = 2k$ the star is not the only extremal family: choosing one set from each complementary pair $\{A, [n]\setminus A\}$ also gives $\frac12\binom{2k}{k} = \binom{2k-1}{k-1}$ sets.
- Intersecting (no two disjoint) and pairwise disjoint are opposite conditions; the sunflower lemma uses the second inside its proof.
- In the sunflower lemma the sets must be distinct and all of the same size $k$, and the core may be empty.

- [[hypergraphs]]: a family of $k$-element sets is a $k$-uniform hypergraph, and Erdős–Ko–Rado is a Turán-type theorem for hypergraphs: it bounds the number of edges when two disjoint edges are forbidden.
- [[probabilistic-method]]: the chain-counting proof of LYM is a random-permutation argument, and the sunflower bounds of 2019 come from a probabilistic analysis.
- [[p-vs-np]]: Razborov's 1985 superpolynomial lower bound for monotone circuits computing the clique function used the sunflower lemma, and Alon and Boppana strengthened it to an exponential bound; this is one of the ways set systems enter complexity theory.
- Coding theory treats codes as families of subsets (binary words) with distance restrictions, and many bounds there have the same flavour.
- The union-closed sets conjecture of Frankl (if a finite family is closed under unions and has a nonempty member, some element lies in at least half the members) is a famous open problem of this type; Gilmer proved in 2022 that some element lies in a constant fraction of the members.

2. A family of subsets of $[n]$ contains no three sets $A \subsetneq B \subsetneq C$. Adapt the chain-counting proof to show that its size is at most the sum of the two largest binomial coefficients $\binom{n}{j}$.

blocks.body:
A graph records which pairs of objects are related. Many structures relate larger groups: the lines of a finite geometry are triples of points, the clauses of a logic formula are sets of variables, the arithmetic progressions of length 3 in $\{1, \dots, N\}$ are triples of numbers. A hypergraph allows edges with any number of vertices.

The classical questions about graphs (how many edges force a given subgraph, how large must a structure be before a colouring has a monochromatic piece) make sense for hypergraphs, but they become dramatically harder. The simplest unsolved case is striking: nobody knows how many triples on $n$ points can be chosen with no four points spanning all four of their triples.

blocks.title: Hypergraph
blocks.body:
A hypergraph $H$ consists of a finite vertex set $V$ and a family $E$ of subsets of $V$, called edges. It is $k$-uniform (a $k$-graph) if every edge has exactly $k$ vertices. The complete $k$-graph $K_n^{(k)}$ has all $\binom nk$ $k$-subsets of an $n$-set as edges.

So a 2-graph is an ordinary graph (see [[graph-basics]]), and a $k$-graph is the same thing as a family of $k$-element sets, the object of [[set-systems]]. The tetrahedron $K_4^{(3)}$ is the 3-graph on four vertices whose edges are all four triples.

blocks.title: From Turán's theorem to Turán densities
blocks.body:
For graphs, Mantel's theorem says that a triangle-free graph on $n$ vertices has at most $\lfloor n^2/4 \rfloor$ edges, attained by the complete bipartite graph with parts as equal as possible. Turán's theorem generalises this: a graph with no $K_{r+1}$ has at most a fraction $1 - \frac1r$ of all possible edges, asymptotically, and the extremal graph is complete $r$-partite with equal parts (see [[extremal-graphs]]). The Erdős–Stone–Simonovits theorem extends this to every forbidden graph.

For $k$-graphs the natural analogue is the following.

blocks.title: Turán number and Turán density
blocks.body:
For a $k$-graph $F$, the Turán number $\mathrm{ex}(n, F)$ is the largest number of edges in a $k$-graph on $n$ vertices that contains no copy of $F$. The Turán density is
$$\pi(F) = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{\mathrm{ex}(n,F)}{\binom nk}.$$
It is the largest fraction of all $k$-sets that an $F$-free $k$-graph can contain, for large $n$.

blocks.title: Averaging lemma (Katona–Nemetz–Simonovits, 1964)
blocks.body:
For every $k$-graph $F$ and every $n > k$,
$$\frac{\mathrm{ex}(n,F)}{\binom nk} \le \frac{\mathrm{ex}(n-1,F)}{\binom{n-1}k}.$$
So the ratio is non-increasing in $n$ and, being bounded below by 0, has a limit; $\pi(F)$ is well defined.

Let $H$ be an $F$-free $k$-graph on $n$ vertices with $\mathrm{ex}(n,F)$ edges. Deleting one vertex leaves an $F$-free $k$-graph on $n-1$ vertices, with at most $\mathrm{ex}(n-1,F)$ edges. Sum over the $n$ choices of the deleted vertex. An edge survives exactly when the deleted vertex is not one of its $k$ vertices, which happens for $n - k$ choices. Double counting gives
$$(n-k)\,\mathrm{ex}(n,F) \le n\,\mathrm{ex}(n-1,F).$$
Since $\binom nk = \frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-1}{k}$, dividing both sides by $(n-k)\binom nk = n\binom{n-1}k$ gives the inequality.

blocks.title: The tetrahedron problem
blocks.body:
For the tetrahedron, start with the smallest case: on 4 vertices, a $K_4^{(3)}$-free 3-graph can have 3 of the 4 triples, so $\mathrm{ex}(4, K_4^{(3)}) = 3$ and the averaging lemma gives $\pi(K_4^{(3)}) \le \frac34$.

In 1941 Turán proposed the following construction. Split the vertices into three parts $V_1, V_2, V_3$ of nearly equal size. Take as edges every triple with one vertex in each part, and every triple with two vertices in $V_i$ and one in $V_{i+1}$, indices taken cyclically ($V_4 = V_1$). The first example below checks that it contains no tetrahedron and has density tending to $\frac59$. Turán conjectured that this is optimal:
$$\pi\big(K_4^{(3)}\big) \overset{?}{=} \tfrac59.$$
This is still open. Chung and Lu proved $\pi(K_4^{(3)}) \le \frac{3+\sqrt{17}}{12} \approx 0.5936$ in 1999. In 2010 Razborov used his flag algebra method, which turns the problem into a large semidefinite program solved by computer, to show $\pi(K_4^{(3)}) \le 0.561666$; later flag-algebra computations have lowered this slightly. The gap to $\frac59 = 0.5555\ldots$ is small but has resisted every approach.

One reason for the difficulty is that, unlike for graphs, there are many different near-extremal constructions: Brown, Kostochka and Fon-der-Flaass found many non-isomorphic 3-graphs achieving the same density $\frac59$. A proof cannot simply show that an extremal hypergraph must look like one particular object.

Some hypergraph Turán densities are known. Erdős showed in 1964 that $\pi(F) = 0$ exactly when $F$ is $k$-partite (its vertices split into $k$ classes with every edge meeting each class once). For the Fano plane, de Caen and Füredi proved in 2000 that the density is $\frac34$ (see the third example).

blocks.title: Colouring hypergraphs
blocks.body: A hypergraph is 2-colourable (has property B) if its vertices can be coloured red and blue so that no edge is monochromatic. For graphs this just means bipartite. For $k$-graphs, the question is how many edges are needed to make a 2-colouring impossible.

blocks.title: Erdős's property B bound (1963)
blocks.body: Every $k$-uniform hypergraph with fewer than $2^{k-1}$ edges is 2-colourable.

Colour each vertex red or blue independently with probability $\frac12$. A fixed edge has $k$ vertices, so it is all red with probability $2^{-k}$ and all blue with probability $2^{-k}$, monochromatic with probability $2^{1-k}$. If there are $m < 2^{k-1}$ edges, the union bound gives
$$\Pr[\text{some edge monochromatic}] \le m \cdot 2^{1-k} < 1,$$
so some colouring has no monochromatic edge. (This is the [[probabilistic-method]] in its simplest form.)

blocks.title: Ramsey numbers for hypergraphs
blocks.body:
Ramsey's theorem holds for $k$-sets (see [[ramsey]]): for every $s$ and $t$ there is a least $r_k(s,t)$ such that every red/blue colouring of the edges of $K_n^{(k)}$, for $n \ge r_k(s,t)$, contains a red $K_s^{(k)}$ or a blue $K_t^{(k)}$. For $k = 2$ these are the usual Ramsey numbers, which grow exponentially. For $k = 3$, Erdős, Hajnal and Rado showed
$$2^{c s^2} < r_3(s,s) < 2^{2^{c' s}}$$
for constants $c, c' > 0$. Whether the true growth is a single or a double exponential is a well-known open problem, and very few exact values are known: one of them is $r_3(4,4) = 13$, proved by McKay and Radziszowski in 1991 with a large computer search.

blocks.title: Why hypergraphs matter beyond themselves
blocks.body:
Many problems about integers can be encoded as problems about hypergraphs: the 3-term arithmetic progressions in a set of integers form a 3-graph, and a set with no progressions corresponds to a 3-graph with very few edges of a certain kind. Two modern tools exploit this.

- Hypergraph regularity. Szemerédi's regularity lemma for graphs says every large graph is approximately a union of a bounded number of random-like bipartite pieces. In the mid-2000s Gowers, and independently Rödl and his coauthors (Nagle, Schacht, Skokan), proved hypergraph versions together with the matching counting lemmas. A consequence is the hypergraph removal lemma, which gives new proofs of Szemerédi's theorem on arithmetic progressions and its multidimensional versions (see [[arithmetic-progressions]]).
- Containers. Balogh, Morris and Samotij, and independently Saxton and Thomason (both published in 2015), showed that the independent sets of a hypergraph with well-spread edges are all contained in a small number of containers, each with few edges. This gives counting results (for example for sum-free sets) and versions of Turán and Szemerédi theorems inside random sets.

blocks.title: Turán's construction
blocks.body: Show that Turán's 3-graph described above contains no $K_4^{(3)}$, and that when the three parts have size $m$ each its density tends to $\frac59$ as $m \to \infty$.
blocks.solution:
Take any 4 vertices; we find a triple among them that is not an edge. Record how many of the 4 vertices lie in each part.

- If some part contains 3 of them, those 3 form a non-edge (no edge has three vertices in one part).
- If the pattern is $2, 2, 0$, with two vertices in $V_i$ and two in $V_j$: with three parts, exactly one of $j = i + 1$ and $i = j + 1$ holds (cyclically). If $j = i+1$, then the triple with two vertices in $V_j$ and one in $V_i$ is a non-edge; otherwise the triple with two in $V_i$ and one in $V_j$ is.
- If the pattern is $2, 1, 1$, with two vertices in $V_i$ and one each in $V_{i+1}$ and $V_{i+2}$: the triple consisting of the two vertices in $V_i$ and the one in $V_{i+2}$ is not an edge, because two vertices in $V_i$ must be completed from $V_{i+1}$.

So every 4-set misses a triple, and there is no tetrahedron.

With parts of size $m$, there are $m^3$ triples meeting all three parts, and for each $i$ there are $\binom m2 \cdot m$ triples with two vertices in $V_i$ and one in $V_{i+1}$. The number of edges is
$$m^3 + 3m\binom m2 = m^3 + \tfrac32 m^2(m-1) \sim \tfrac52 m^3,$$
while $\binom{3m}{3} \sim \frac{27}{6}m^3 = \frac92 m^3$. The ratio tends to $\frac{5/2}{9/2} = \frac59$. Hence $\pi(K_4^{(3)}) \ge \frac59$. For finite $m$ the ratio is larger (it is $0.7$ for $m = 2$ and $\frac{54}{84} \approx 0.643$ for $m = 3$), consistent with the averaging lemma.

blocks.title: Exact values on few vertices
blocks.body: Use the averaging lemma to show $\mathrm{ex}(5, K_4^{(3)}) \le 7$, and find a $K_4^{(3)}$-free 3-graph on 5 vertices with 7 edges.
blocks.solution:
We know $\mathrm{ex}(4, K_4^{(3)}) = 3$. The lemma, in the form $(n-k)\,\mathrm{ex}(n,F) \le n\,\mathrm{ex}(n-1,F)$ with $n = 5$, $k = 3$, gives $2\,\mathrm{ex}(5, K_4^{(3)}) \le 15$, so $\mathrm{ex}(5, K_4^{(3)}) \le 7$.

Turán's construction with parts $V_1 = \{a, b\}$, $V_2 = \{c, d\}$, $V_3 = \{e\}$ attains this. Its edges are the 4 triples with one vertex in each part ($ace, ade, bce, bde$), the triples $abc$, $abd$ (two in $V_1$, one in $V_2$), and $cde$ (two in $V_2$, one in $V_3$): 7 edges in total, and the first example shows it has no tetrahedron. So $\mathrm{ex}(5, K_4^{(3)}) = 7$.

blocks.title: The Fano plane
blocks.body: The Fano plane is the 3-graph on vertices $\{0, 1, \dots, 6\}$ whose 7 edges (lines) are $\{0,1,2\}, \{0,3,4\}, \{0,5,6\}, \{1,3,5\}, \{1,4,6\}, \{2,3,6\}, \{2,4,5\}$. Every two vertices lie on exactly one line, and every two lines meet in exactly one vertex. Show that the Fano plane is not 2-colourable, and deduce that $\pi(\text{Fano}) \ge \frac34$.
blocks.solution:
Suppose the 7 vertices are coloured red and blue. One colour, say red, has at least 4 vertices.

If red has at least 5 vertices, choose 5 red vertices and let $u, v$ be the other two vertices (whatever their colours). Each vertex lies on 3 lines, and exactly one line contains both $u$ and $v$, so the number of lines through $u$ or $v$ is $3 + 3 - 1 = 5$. The remaining $7 - 5 = 2$ lines avoid $u$ and $v$ and therefore consist of red vertices.

If red has exactly 4 vertices, the blue set $B$ has 3. If $B$ is a line, it is a blue line. If not, count the lines meeting $B$: each of its 3 points lies on 3 lines, each of the 3 pairs in $B$ lies on exactly one common line, and no line contains all of $B$. By inclusion–exclusion $9 - 3 + 0 = 6$ lines meet $B$, so one line avoids $B$ and is red.

In every case some line is monochromatic, so the Fano plane does not have property B.

For the density: split $n$ vertices into two halves $A$, $B$ and take as edges all triples that meet both halves. This 3-graph contains no Fano plane, because a copy would be 2-coloured by the halves with no monochromatic line. Its number of edges is $\binom n3 - \binom{|A|}3 - \binom{|B|}3$, and with $|A| = |B| = n/2$ the ratio to $\binom n3$ tends to $1 - 2 \cdot \frac18 = \frac34$. De Caen and Füredi proved that $\frac34$ is the exact value.

blocks.title: Triples that share at most one point
blocks.body: A 3-graph is linear if any two edges share at most one vertex. Show that a linear 3-graph on $n$ vertices has at most $n(n-1)/6$ edges, and that equality forces $n \equiv 1$ or $3 \pmod 6$.
blocks.solution:
Each edge contains 3 pairs of vertices, and by linearity no pair lies in two edges. So $3e \le \binom n2$, that is $e \le n(n-1)/6$.

Equality means every pair lies in exactly one edge; such a 3-graph is a Steiner triple system. Fix a vertex $v$. The $n-1$ pairs $\{v, w\}$ are each covered by exactly one edge through $v$, and each edge through $v$ covers two of them, so $n - 1$ is even and $n$ is odd. Also $n(n-1)/6$ must be an integer, so $3 \mid n(n-1)$, that is $n \equiv 0$ or $1 \pmod 3$. Combined with $n$ odd this gives $n \equiv 1$ or $3 \pmod 6$.

The Fano plane is the case $n = 7$, and the 12 lines of the $3 \times 3$ grid over $\mathbb Z/3$ (rows, columns and the two families of wrapped diagonals) give $n = 9$. Kirkman showed in 1847 that Steiner triple systems exist for every $n \equiv 1, 3 \pmod 6$.

blocks.body:
- $K_4^{(3)}$ is not the graph $K_4$: it has 4 vertices and 4 edges, each a triple. A 3-graph can contain all six pairs of four vertices inside its edges without containing $K_4^{(3)}$.
- The Turán density is normalised by $\binom nk$, not by $n^k$; the two conventions differ by a factor $k!$.
- Colouring a hypergraph usually means colouring vertices (property B), whereas Ramsey problems colour edges. Keep track of which is meant.
- Graph intuition can mislead. For graphs, $\pi(F)$ depends only on the chromatic number of $F$, and for non-bipartite $F$ all near-extremal graphs are close to a single Turán graph; for 3-graphs there is no such formula, and the tetrahedron has many very different constructions with the conjectured extremal density.

- [[set-systems]]: the Erdős–Ko–Rado theorem is the Turán problem for $k$-graphs whose forbidden configuration is two disjoint edges.
- [[extremal-graphs]]: Turán's theorem and the Erdős–Stone–Simonovits theorem are the $k = 2$ case, completely solved.
- [[ramsey]] and [[infinite-combinatorics]]: Ramsey's theorem for $k$-sets, with tower-type bounds.
- [[probabilistic-method]]: random colourings give property B bounds, and the local lemma 2-colours hypergraphs whose edges overlap little.
- [[arithmetic-progressions]] and [[additive-combinatorics]]: hypergraph regularity and removal give Szemerédi-type theorems, and containers count sets avoiding additive patterns.
- [[discrete-geometry]]: incidence structures such as points and lines are hypergraphs, and the Erdős–Szekeres theorem uses Ramsey's theorem for 4-element sets.

blocks.body:
Can a chessboard with two opposite corners cut off be covered by dominoes? Can a $10 \times 10$ board be covered by $1 \times 4$ strips? Which single square can be removed from an $8 \times 8$ board so that the rest can be covered by $1 \times 3$ strips? Grid problems like these are a staple of olympiads, and most impossibility proofs in this area use the same trick: colour the board so that every tile covers the colours in a fixed proportion, then count.

The colouring is an invariant in disguise (see [[invariants]]): however the tiles are placed, the number of cells of each colour covered so far changes in a predictable way. When the board's colour counts do not fit that pattern, no tiling exists.

blocks.title: The mutilated chessboard
blocks.body: An $8 \times 8$ board has 64 cells; remove two opposite corners and 62 remain, an even number, so counting area alone does not rule out a tiling by 31 dominoes. Colour the board in the usual chessboard pattern. Two opposite corners have the same colour: corner $(1,1)$ and corner $(8,8)$ both have $i + j$ even. So the mutilated board has 30 cells of one colour and 32 of the other.

blocks.title: Mutilated chessboard
blocks.body: A mutilated $8 \times 8$ board (two opposite corners removed) has no domino tiling.

Colour cell $(i,j)$ black if $i + j$ is even and white otherwise. Two horizontally or vertically adjacent cells differ by 1 in exactly one coordinate, so every domino covers one black and one white cell. A tiling by 31 dominoes would therefore cover 31 black and 31 white cells. But the removed corners $(1,1)$ and $(8,8)$ are both black, so the mutilated board has $32 - 2 = 30$ black cells and $32$ white cells. No tiling exists.

blocks.title: When the colours balance
blocks.body:
The colouring argument gives a necessary condition: a region tileable by dominoes has as many black as white cells. It is not sufficient in general. The region below has 6 cells, 3 of each colour, but cannot be tiled: the top cell and the left cell are both adjacent only to the same cell of the long row, and they cannot both use it.

$$\begin{array}{cccc} & \square & & \\ \square & \square & \square & \square \\ & & \square & \end{array}$$

For the full board, however, balance is enough. This is a theorem usually credited to Ralph Gomory.

blocks.title: Gomory's theorem
blocks.body: If one black and one white cell are removed from an $8 \times 8$ chessboard, the remaining 62 cells can always be tiled by dominoes.

Find a closed path through all 64 cells that moves between adjacent cells. One such path: start at the top-left corner and go right along row 1 to its end; go down one step into row 2 and snake through rows 2 to 8 using only columns 2 to 8 (row 2 right to left, row 3 left to right, and so on, ending in row 8 at column 2); step left into column 1 and climb column 1 back up to row 2, then step to the starting cell. Every cell is visited exactly once, and the last cell, in column 1 of row 2, is adjacent to the first.

Along this cycle the colours alternate, since consecutive cells are adjacent. Remove a black cell $b$ and a white cell $w$. They cut the cycle into two arcs (one of them empty if $b$ and $w$ are neighbours on the cycle). Walking from $b$ to $w$ along the cycle, the colours go black, white, black, ..., and since $w$ is white it is an odd number of steps from $b$; so each arc strictly between them contains an even number of cells. Cover each arc by dominoes, pairing its cells in order: each pair consists of consecutive cells on the cycle, which are adjacent on the board. This tiles the 62 remaining cells.

blocks.title: Colourings for longer tiles
blocks.body:
For a $1 \times k$ strip, two colours are not enough. Use $k$ colours along diagonals: give cell $(i,j)$ the colour $(i + j) \bmod k$. A horizontal or vertical strip of length $k$ covers $k$ consecutive values of $i+j$, hence exactly one cell of each colour. So a region tileable by $1 \times k$ strips has the same number of cells of each colour.

An equivalent and often more convenient way to write this uses complex numbers (see [[complex-numbers]]). Let $\zeta = e^{2\pi i/k}$ and give cell $(i,j)$ the weight $\zeta^{i+j}$. A strip starting at $(i,j)$ has total weight $\zeta^{i+j}(1 + \zeta + \dots + \zeta^{k-1}) = 0$. So a tileable region has total weight $0$. This weighting gives a complete answer for rectangles.

blocks.title: Rectangles tiled by strips
blocks.body: Let $k \ge 2$. An $a \times b$ rectangle can be tiled by $1 \times k$ strips (in either orientation) if and only if $k \mid a$ or $k \mid b$.

If $k \mid a$, fill each of the $b$ columns of height $a$ with vertical strips; if $k \mid b$, fill each row with horizontal strips.

Conversely, suppose a tiling exists. Index the cells by $0 \le i < a$, $0 \le j < b$ and weight them by $\zeta^{i+j}$. Each strip has weight 0, so the whole rectangle does:
$$0 = \sum_{i=0}^{a-1}\sum_{j=0}^{b-1} \zeta^{i+j} = \Big(\sum_{i=0}^{a-1}\zeta^i\Big)\Big(\sum_{j=0}^{b-1}\zeta^j\Big) = \frac{1-\zeta^a}{1-\zeta}\cdot\frac{1-\zeta^b}{1-\zeta}.$$
A product of complex numbers is zero only if a factor is zero, so $\zeta^a = 1$ or $\zeta^b = 1$, which means $k \mid a$ or $k \mid b$.

blocks.title: Counting tilings
blocks.body:
Besides asking whether a tiling exists, one can ask how many there are. A $2 \times n$ strip has $F_{n+1}$ domino tilings, where $F$ are the Fibonacci numbers (first example). For general boards the count is much harder, but for dominoes there is a remarkable formula. Domino tilings of a region are the same as perfect matchings of its grid graph (see [[cycles-matchings]]), and in 1961 Kasteleyn, and independently Temperley and Fisher, showed that for planar regions this number can be computed as a determinant of a suitably signed adjacency matrix (see [[determinants]]). For the $8 \times 8$ board the answer is $12\,988\,816$.

This connection is the starting point of the dimer model in statistical physics, where random domino tilings of large regions show striking large-scale behaviour.

blocks.title: Domino tilings of a 2 by n strip
blocks.body: Let $t_n$ be the number of domino tilings of a $2 \times n$ rectangle. Show that $t_n = F_{n+1}$, where $F_1 = F_2 = 1$ and $F_{m+1} = F_m + F_{m-1}$.
blocks.solution: Look at the leftmost column. Either it is covered by one vertical domino, leaving a $2 \times (n-1)$ strip, or its top cell is covered by a horizontal domino; then the bottom cell must also be covered by a horizontal domino directly below, and a $2 \times (n-2)$ strip remains. These cases are disjoint, so $t_n = t_{n-1} + t_{n-2}$ for $n \ge 2$, with $t_0 = 1$ (the empty tiling) and $t_1 = 1$. These are the Fibonacci initial values shifted by one, so $t_n = F_{n+1}$. For example $t_4 = 5$ and $t_8 = 34$.

blocks.title: A 10 by 10 board and 1 by 4 strips
blocks.body: Show that a $10 \times 10$ board cannot be tiled by $1 \times 4$ strips, using a colour count.
blocks.solution:
This follows from the theorem on rectangles, since $4 \nmid 10$, but it is instructive to see the colour count directly. Colour cell $(i,j)$, $0 \le i, j \le 9$, with $(i+j) \bmod 4$. Each strip covers one cell of each colour, so 25 strips would cover exactly 25 cells of each colour.

Count the colours. Among $0, 1, \dots, 9$ the residues $0, 1, 2, 3$ modulo 4 occur $n_0 = 3$, $n_1 = 3$, $n_2 = 2$, $n_3 = 2$ times, for $i$ and for $j$ alike. The number of cells of colour $c$ is $\sum_r n_r\, n_{c-r}$ (indices mod 4):
$$\begin{aligned} \text{colour } 0 &: n_0n_0 + n_1n_3 + n_2n_2 + n_3n_1 = 9 + 6 + 4 + 6 = 25,\\ \text{colour } 1 &: n_0n_1 + n_1n_0 + n_2n_3 + n_3n_2 = 9 + 9 + 4 + 4 = 26,\\ \text{colour } 2 &: n_0n_2 + n_1n_1 + n_2n_0 + n_3n_3 = 6 + 9 + 6 + 4 = 25,\\ \text{colour } 3 &: n_0n_3 + n_1n_2 + n_2n_1 + n_3n_0 = 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 = 24. \end{aligned}$$
The counts are not all equal, so no tiling exists.

blocks.title: Removing one cell for 1 by 3 strips
blocks.body: One cell is removed from an $8 \times 8$ board, and the remaining 63 cells are to be tiled by 21 strips of size $1 \times 3$. Which cells can be removed?
blocks.solution:
Number rows and columns $1, \dots, 8$ and use two colourings: $c_1(i,j) = (i + j) \bmod 3$ and $c_2(i,j) = (i - j) \bmod 3$. A strip covers three cells along a row or column, so for each colouring it covers one cell of each colour. Hence after removal each colouring must show exactly 21 cells of each colour.

Among $1, \dots, 8$, the residues $1$ and $2$ modulo 3 occur three times each and the residue $0$ twice. For $c_1$, colour 0 has $2\cdot 2 + 3\cdot 3 + 3 \cdot 3 = 22$ cells (pairs of residues $(0,0), (1,2), (2,1)$) and the other two colours have 21 each. The same computation gives 22 cells with $c_2 = 0$ and 21 for each other colour. So the removed cell must have $i + j \equiv 0$ and $i - j \equiv 0 \pmod 3$. Adding, $2i \equiv 0$, so $i \equiv 0$ and then $j \equiv 0 \pmod 3$. The only candidates are $(3,3), (3,6), (6,3), (6,6)$.

These four cells are images of each other under rotations of the board, so it suffices to tile the board with $(3,3)$ removed. Rows 6 to 8 form a $3 \times 8$ block, tiled by 8 vertical strips. In rows 1 to 5, columns 6 to 8 form a $5 \times 3$ block, tiled by 5 horizontal strips. What is left is the $5 \times 5$ square in rows 1 to 5 and columns 1 to 5 with its centre $(3,3)$ removed. That ring splits into four $2 \times 3$ rectangles arranged like a pinwheel: rows 1–2 with columns 1–3, rows 1–3 with columns 4–5, rows 4–5 with columns 3–5, and rows 3–5 with columns 1–2. Each $2 \times 3$ rectangle is two parallel strips. So exactly the four cells $(3,3), (3,6), (6,3), (6,6)$ work.

blocks.title: L-trominoes on a 2^n board
blocks.body: Prove that for every $n \ge 1$ and every cell of a $2^n \times 2^n$ board, the board with that cell removed can be tiled by L-shaped trominoes (three cells forming a $2 \times 2$ square minus one cell).
blocks.solution:
Induction on $n$. For $n = 1$, a $2 \times 2$ board minus one cell is itself an L-tromino.

Suppose the statement holds for $2^{n-1} \times 2^{n-1}$ boards. Split the $2^n \times 2^n$ board into four quadrants of that size. The removed cell lies in one quadrant. Place one L-tromino at the centre of the board so that it covers the corner cell, at the centre, of each of the other three quadrants. Now each of the four quadrants has exactly one cell that is missing or already covered, and by the induction hypothesis each can be tiled by L-trominoes. Together with the central tromino this tiles the whole board minus the chosen cell.

Note that $4^n - 1$ is divisible by 3, as it must be. Divisibility of the area by 3 alone does not guarantee a tiling: a $3 \times 3$ square cannot be tiled by three L-trominoes.

blocks.body:
- A colour count proves impossibility only. Equal counts do not prove that a tiling exists (see the six-cell region above); for existence you need a construction.
- Check that every placement of every tile, in all orientations allowed, covers the colours in the same proportions. The diagonal colouring mod $k$ works for straight strips but not for L-shapes.
- Count the colours of the board carefully, and remember that which colour has the extra cell depends on the board's dimensions modulo the number of colours.
- Different colourings rule out different cells; in the $1 \times 3$ problem one colouring alone leaves 22 candidate cells, and only the combination of two colourings narrows it to four.

- [[invariants]]: a colouring argument is an invariant (the colour counts covered so far) that every move preserves.
- [[cycles-matchings]] and [[graph-basics]]: domino tilings are perfect matchings of grid graphs, and Gomory's proof uses a Hamiltonian cycle.
- [[determinants]]: the Kasteleyn–Temperley–Fisher method counts domino tilings of planar regions as determinants.
- [[complex-numbers]]: roots-of-unity weights turn colouring arguments into algebra.
- [[generating-functions]]: tiling counts of strips satisfy linear recurrences, as the Fibonacci example shows.
- [[comb-games]]: board colourings also decide many pursuit and placement games.

1. Can a $6 \times 6$ board be tiled by $1 \times 4$ strips? Can a $4 \times 6$ board?
2. Show that a $5 \times 5$ board with one cell removed can be tiled by dominoes if and only if the removed cell has the same colour as the corners.
3. Prove that a $3 \times 3$ square cannot be tiled by L-trominoes.
4. Show that the number of tilings of a $3 \times n$ rectangle by dominoes is $0$ for odd $n$, and find a recurrence for even $n$.

sources.ref: Golomb, Polyominoes: Puzzles, Patterns, Problems, and Packings
Kasteleyn, The statistics of dimers on a lattice, Physica 27 (1961)
