blocks.body:
Put $n$ points in the plane. How many pairs can be at distance exactly 1? How few different distances can the pairs determine? Must some of the points form a convex pentagon? Must some line pass through exactly two of them? Combinatorial geometry asks such questions about finite configurations of points, lines and circles, where the answer depends on both counting and geometry.

Many of these problems were posed by Erdős in the 1930s and 1940s. Their elementary statements hide real difficulty: the best answers combine double counting, graph drawing, Ramsey theory and, since 2010, algebraic geometry.

blocks.title: Unit distances and distinct distances
blocks.body:
For a set $P$ of $n$ points, let $u(P)$ be the number of pairs at distance 1 and $g(P)$ the number of distinct distances among all pairs. Write $u(n)$ for the maximum of $u(P)$ and $g(n)$ for the minimum of $g(P)$ over $n$-point sets. The two problems pull in opposite directions: a set with few distinct distances must repeat some distance often.

Simple constructions. Points equally spaced on a line, at $0, 1, \dots, n-1$, give $n - 1$ unit distances and $n - 1$ distinct distances. Doing better takes more care. A square $\sqrt n \times \sqrt n$ grid of integer points determines only about $n/\sqrt{\log n}$ distinct distances, because the squared distances are sums of two squares below $2n$, and few integers have that form (see [[sums-of-squares]]). Scaling the same grid so that its most frequent distance becomes 1, Erdős obtained $u(n) \ge n^{1 + c/\log\log n}$ for a constant $c > 0$.

Elementary upper and lower bounds come from the fact that two distinct circles meet in at most two points.

blocks.title: Elementary distance bounds

blocks.body:
1. For each point $p$, let $d_p$ be the number of points at distance 1 from $p$; then $\sum_p d_p = 2u$. Count triples $(p, \{q, r\})$ with $q, r$ both at distance 1 from $p$. For fixed $p$ there are $\binom{d_p}{2}$ of them. For a fixed pair $\{q, r\}$, the point $p$ lies on the unit circles around $q$ and around $r$, which meet in at most two points. So
$$\sum_p \binom{d_p}{2} \le 2\binom n2 = n(n-1).$$
The function $x \mapsto x(x-1)/2$ is convex, so with $x = 2u/n$ the average degree, $\sum_p \binom{d_p}{2} \ge n\cdot\frac{x(x-1)}{2}$ (see [[convexity]]). Hence $x^2 - x - 2(n-1) \le 0$, so $x \le \frac12\big(1 + \sqrt{8n-7}\big)$ and $u = nx/2 \le \frac n4\big(1 + \sqrt{8n-7}\big)$.

2. Let the distinct distances be $r_1, \dots, r_t$ and fix two points $p \ne q$. Each of the other $n - 2$ points lies on one of the $t$ circles of radius $r_i$ around $p$ and on one of the $t$ circles of radius $r_j$ around $q$. For each of the $t^2$ choices of $(i, j)$ the two circles have different centres and meet in at most 2 points. So $n - 2 \le 2t^2$.

blocks.title: What is known, and a 2026 claim
blocks.body:
Both elementary bounds are far from the truth.

For unit distances, Spencer, Szemerédi and Trotter proved in 1984 that
$$\#\text{unit distances} \le O(n^{4/3}).$$
A short proof found by Székely in 1997 uses the crossing lemma: a graph drawn in the plane with $v$ vertices and $e \ge 4v$ edges has at least $e^3/(64v^2)$ pairs of crossing edges. Applied to the drawing whose vertices are the points and whose edges are arcs of unit circles around them, it gives the $n^{4/3}$ bound. We omit the details. For decades nobody has improved the exponent $4/3$.

Erdős conjectured in 1946 that his grid construction is close to optimal, that is, that $u(n)$ is at most $n^{1+o(1)}$, with a sharper form predicting the order $n^{1 + c/\log\log n}$ of the grid. On 20 May 2026 it was reported that an internal OpenAI model had found a counterexample to Erdős's unit distance conjecture, and that Tim Gowers had praised the proof. This is a recent claim, not an established result, and this lesson does not say which form of the conjecture it would refute or what bound it would give.

For distinct distances, Erdős conjectured that the grid is optimal up to constants, $g(n) \ge c\,n/\sqrt{\log n}$. In 2010 Guth and Katz proved
$$\#\text{distinct distances} \ge c\,\frac{n}{\log n},$$
which misses the conjecture by only a factor $\sqrt{\log n}$. Their proof translates the problem, following an idea of Elekes and Sharir, into counting intersections of lines in three-dimensional space, and then bounds those using polynomial partitioning (a polynomial of controlled degree whose zero set cuts space into cells each containing few lines), together with classical facts about ruled surfaces to handle the lines that lie inside the zero set.

blocks.title: Incidences between points and lines
blocks.body: An incidence between a set of points and a set of lines is a pair (point, line) with the point on the line. With $m$ points and $n$ lines, a Cauchy–Schwarz argument gives at most about $m\sqrt n + n$ incidences (third example). The truth is smaller.

blocks.title: Szemerédi–Trotter theorem (1983)
blocks.body:
There is a constant $C$ such that $m$ points and $n$ lines in the plane have at most
$$C\big(m^{2/3}n^{2/3} + m + n\big)$$
incidences.

blocks.title: About the Szemerédi–Trotter theorem
blocks.body: The proof is omitted; Székely's crossing-lemma argument gives it in a page. The bound is sharp up to the constant: with points the integer grid $\{1,\dots,k\} \times \{1,\dots,2k^2\}$ and lines $y = ax + b$ with $a \in \{1,\dots,k\}$, $b \in \{1,\dots,k^2\}$, each line contains $k$ grid points, giving $k^4$ incidences among $2k^3$ points and $k^3$ lines, which is of order $m^{2/3}n^{2/3}$. Unit distances are an incidence problem between points and unit circles, which is why the same exponent $4/3$ appears.

blocks.title: Convex position: the Erdős–Szekeres theorem
blocks.body: A set of points is in general position if no three are collinear, and in convex position if each point is a vertex of the convex hull of the set. Esther Klein observed that among any 5 points in general position, 4 are in convex position (second example). Erdős and Szekeres asked how many points force $k$ points in convex position; the story is known as the happy ending problem, because Klein and Szekeres later married.

blocks.title: Erdős–Szekeres theorem (1935)
blocks.body:
For every $k \ge 3$ there is a least integer $f(k)$ such that every set of $f(k)$ points in general position in the plane contains $k$ points in convex position. Moreover
$$2^{k-2} + 1 \le f(k) \le \binom{2k-4}{k-2} + 1.$$

blocks.title: Proof that f(k) exists
blocks.body:
We prove existence using Ramsey's theorem for 4-element subsets (see [[ramsey]]); the explicit bounds need finer arguments and are not proved here.

First, if every 4 points of a finite set $S$ in general position are in convex position, then $S$ is in convex position. Otherwise some point $p \in S$ is not a vertex of the convex hull of $S$, so it lies in that hull. Triangulate the hull by joining one hull vertex to all others; $p$ lies in one of these triangles, whose vertices are three points of $S$, and by general position it is in the interior. Those three points together with $p$ are not in convex position.

Now colour each 4-element subset of a large point set red if it is in convex position and blue otherwise. By Ramsey's theorem there is an $N$ such that any such colouring of the 4-subsets of $N$ points has a 5-set all of whose 4-subsets are blue or a $k$-set all of whose 4-subsets are red. The first is impossible by Klein's observation. So there are $k$ points all of whose 4-subsets are convex, and by the previous paragraph they are in convex position.

blocks.title: The current state
blocks.body:
The lower bound $2^{k-2} + 1$ comes from an explicit construction of Erdős and Szekeres (1961), who conjectured it is exact. Small cases agree: $f(4) = 5$ by Klein's observation, $f(5) = 9$, and $f(6) = 17$, the last by a computer search of Szekeres and Peters (2006). In 2017 Andrew Suk proved $f(k) \le 2^{k + o(k)}$, so the conjecture is now known to be right in the exponent.

Another classic of the subject concerns lines rather than distances.

blocks.title: Sylvester–Gallai theorem
blocks.body: If a finite set of points in the plane is not contained in a line, then some line passes through exactly two of the points.

blocks.title: Kelly's proof
blocks.body:
Call a line connecting if it passes through at least two of the points. Consider all pairs $(P, \ell)$ where $\ell$ is a connecting line and $P$ is a point of the set not on $\ell$; such pairs exist because the points are not collinear, and there are finitely many. Choose a pair for which the distance from $P$ to $\ell$ is smallest, and let $Q$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to $\ell$.

Suppose $\ell$ contains at least three of the points. The point $Q$ divides $\ell$ into two closed rays, so by [[pigeonhole]] two of the points, $A$ and $B$, lie on the same ray; name them so that $|QB| \le |QA|$. Then $A \ne Q$ and $B$ lies on the segment $QA$ (possibly $B = Q$).

Let $m$ be the connecting line $PA$. The point $B$ is not on $m$, since otherwise $m$ would be $\ell$ and $P$ would lie on $\ell$. As a point moves along the segment from $Q$ to $A$, its distance to the line $PA$ decreases in proportion to its distance from $A$, so the distance from $B$ to $m$ is at most the distance from $Q$ to $m$. In the right triangle $PQA$, the distance from $Q$ to the hypotenuse $PA$ equals $|PQ|\cdot|QA|/|PA|$, and $|QA| < |PA|$, so this distance is less than $|PQ|$. Hence the pair $(B, m)$ has smaller distance than $(P, \ell)$, a contradiction. So $\ell$ contains exactly two of the points.

blocks.title: Many unit distances from a cube
blocks.body: Show that for every $k$ there is a set of $n = 2^k$ points in the plane with at least $k\,2^{k-1} = \frac n2 \log_2 n$ unit distances. So $u(n)$ grows faster than any linear function.
blocks.solution:
Choose unit vectors $v_1, \dots, v_k$ in the plane and, for each subset $S \subseteq \{1, \dots, k\}$, the point $x_S = \sum_{i \in S} v_i$. If the directions are chosen generically (for instance at random), the $2^k$ points $x_S$ are distinct, since a coincidence $x_S = x_T$ is a nontrivial linear relation among the $v_i$ with coefficients $0, \pm 1$, and each such relation fails for almost every choice.

If $T = S \cup \{i\}$ with $i \notin S$, then $x_T - x_S = v_i$ has length 1. Each of the $2^k$ subsets $T$ has $|T|$ such neighbours $S$ below it, so the number of these pairs is $\sum_T |T| = k\,2^{k-1}$. All of them are unit distances (there may be more).

This is the planar shadow of the $k$-dimensional cube, whose $k\,2^{k-1}$ edges all have the same length.

blocks.title: Klein's five-point lemma
blocks.body: Prove that among any 5 points in the plane, no three collinear, some 4 are the vertices of a convex quadrilateral.
blocks.solution:
Look at the convex hull. If it has 5 or 4 vertices, any 4 hull vertices are in convex position.

Otherwise the hull is a triangle $ABC$ and the other two points $D$, $E$ lie inside it. The line $DE$ passes through no vertex of the triangle (no three points are collinear), so it leaves the three vertices on its two sides, and by pigeonhole two of them, say $A$ and $B$, are on the same side.

We claim $A, B, D, E$ are in convex position, that is, none of them lies inside the triangle of the other three. $A$ is a vertex of triangle $ABC$, which contains $B$, $D$ and $E$, so $A$ cannot lie in the triangle $BDE$; similarly for $B$. If $D$ were inside triangle $ABE$, the line from the vertex $E$ through the interior point $D$ would cross the opposite side $AB$ at an interior point of the segment, putting $A$ and $B$ on opposite sides of line $DE$, contrary to the choice of $A$, $B$. The same argument with $D$ and $E$ exchanged rules out $E$ inside $ABD$. So $ABDE$ (in a suitable order) is a convex quadrilateral.

Four points are not enough: a triangle with one point inside has no convex quadrilateral.

blocks.title: A first incidence bound
blocks.body: Show that $m$ points and $n$ lines in the plane have at most $n + m\sqrt n$ incidences.
blocks.solution:
For each line $\ell$ let $d_\ell$ be the number of points on it, so the number of incidences is $I = \sum_\ell d_\ell$. Count ordered pairs of distinct points lying on a common line: line $\ell$ contributes $d_\ell(d_\ell - 1)$, and each ordered pair of points lies on at most one line, so
$$\sum_\ell d_\ell^2 - I = \sum_\ell d_\ell(d_\ell - 1) \le m(m-1) \le m^2.$$
By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality (see [[cauchy-schwarz]]), $I^2 = \big(\sum_\ell d_\ell\big)^2 \le n\sum_\ell d_\ell^2 \le n(m^2 + I)$. Thus $I^2 - nI - nm^2 \le 0$, and
$$I \le \frac{n + \sqrt{n^2 + 4nm^2}}{2} \le \frac{n + (n + 2m\sqrt n)}{2} = n + m\sqrt n,$$
using $n^2 + 4nm^2 \le (n + 2m\sqrt n)^2$. For $m = n$ this gives $O(n^{3/2})$, compared with the true order $n^{4/3}$ from Szemerédi–Trotter.

blocks.title: Points determine many lines
blocks.body: Prove that $n \ge 3$ points in the plane, not all on one line, determine at least $n$ distinct connecting lines.
blocks.solution:
Induction on $n$. For $n = 3$, three non-collinear points determine 3 lines.

Let $n \ge 4$. By the Sylvester–Gallai theorem there is a line $\ell$ through exactly two of the points, $p$ and $q$. Remove $p$.

If the remaining $n - 1$ points lie on one line $L$, then $p$ is not on $L$ (the original points are not collinear), and the lines from $p$ to each of the $n-1$ points on $L$ are distinct, because each meets $L$ in only one point. Together with $L$ this gives $n$ lines.

Otherwise, by induction the remaining $n - 1$ points determine at least $n - 1$ lines. The line $\ell$ is not among them, because among the remaining points it contains only $q$. So the original set determines at least $n$ lines. (This is a theorem of de Bruijn and Erdős, 1948.)

- Unit-distance and distinct-distance problems point in opposite directions, but they are linked: any distance can be scaled to 1, so each distance occurs at most $u(n)$ times and $g(n) \ge \binom n2 / u(n)$. With the $O(n^{4/3})$ bound this already gives $g(n) \ge c\,n^{2/3}$, far better than the elementary $\sqrt n$.
- General position matters. Without it, all $n$ points could lie on a line, which contains no convex quadrilateral at all.
- The Sylvester–Gallai theorem is special to real geometry and finite sets. Over the complex numbers it fails (the 9 inflection points of a smooth plane cubic have every connecting line through 3 of them), and it fails for infinite sets such as the integer lattice.
- $O(n^{4/3})$ hides a constant; statements like "at most $n^{4/3}$ unit distances" without a constant are not what is proved.
- A reported proof is not the same as an accepted one; recent claims, especially computer- or AI-generated ones, should be cited as claims until independently checked.

- [[ramsey]]: the Erdős–Szekeres theorem is one of the earliest applications of Ramsey's theorem, rediscovered by Szekeres in this context.
- [[probabilistic-method]]: the crossing lemma, which drives Székely's proofs of Szemerédi–Trotter and the unit distance bound, has a short probabilistic proof.
- [[additive-combinatorics]]: Elekes used the Szemerédi–Trotter theorem to prove that a finite set $A$ of reals has $\max(|A+A|, |A\cdot A|) \ge c|A|^{5/4}$, a sum-product estimate.
- [[sums-of-squares]]: the number of distinct distances in a grid is governed by which integers are sums of two squares.
- [[hypergraphs]]: points and lines form a linear hypergraph, and incidence bounds are extremal results for such hypergraphs.
- [[polynomials-roots]]: the polynomial method rests on two simple facts. A polynomial of degree $d$ that vanishes at $d+1$ points of a line vanishes on the whole line, and fewer than $\binom{d+2}{2}$ points in the plane always lie on the zero set of a nonzero polynomial of degree at most $d$, since these polynomials form a vector space of dimension $\binom{d+2}{2}$.

2. Prove that 4 points in the plane determine at most 5 unit distances, and find 4 points with exactly 5.
3. Show that $m$ points and $n$ lines have at most $m + n\sqrt m$ incidences, by exchanging the roles of points and lines in the third example.
4. Show that the Sylvester–Gallai theorem fails for the infinite set $\mathbb Z^2$ of integer points: every line through two of them contains infinitely many.

blocks.body:
Ramsey's theorem says that a large enough finite structure, coloured with a few colours, contains a large monochromatic piece. What if the structure is infinite? For the natural numbers the answer is as good as one could hope: colour the pairs of natural numbers with finitely many colours and there is always an infinite set all of whose pairs have the same colour. For uncountable sets the picture changes completely, and some of the most natural questions cannot be settled from the standard axioms of set theory.

The partition calculus, developed by Erdős, Rado, Hajnal and others from the 1950s on, organises these questions with a single piece of notation, the arrow.

blocks.title: Just enough about infinite cardinals
blocks.body:
Two sets have the same cardinality if there is a bijection between them. The natural numbers have cardinality $\aleph_0$; sets of this size are countable. Cantor showed that the real numbers are not countable; their cardinality is written $2^{\aleph_0}$, since $\mathbb R$ is in bijection with the set of all subsets of $\mathbb N$.

We work in ZFC, the usual axioms of set theory including the axiom of choice. Under choice every set can be well-ordered, and the cardinalities are themselves well-ordered: $\aleph_0 < \aleph_1 < \aleph_2 < \cdots$, where $\aleph_1$ is the smallest uncountable cardinality. A convenient model of a set of size $\aleph_1$ is $\omega_1$, the set of countable ordinals, which is well-ordered in such a way that every element has only countably many predecessors. For a cardinal $\kappa$, $\kappa^+$ denotes the next larger cardinal.

Cantor's theorem gives $2^{\aleph_0} \ge \aleph_1$. The continuum hypothesis (CH) is the statement $2^{\aleph_0} = \aleph_1$. Gödel (1940) showed that ZFC cannot refute CH and Cohen (1963) showed that it cannot prove it: CH is independent of ZFC.

blocks.title: Partition arrow
blocks.body:
For a set $X$ and a positive integer $n$, write $[X]^n$ for the set of all $n$-element subsets of $X$. For cardinals $\kappa, \lambda$ and positive integers $n, r$,
$$\kappa \to (\lambda)^n_r$$
means: for every set $X$ of cardinality $\kappa$ and every colouring $c : [X]^n \to \{1, \dots, r\}$, there is a set $H \subseteq X$ of cardinality $\lambda$ such that $c$ is constant on $[H]^n$. Such an $H$ is called homogeneous for $c$. The negation is written $\kappa \not\to (\lambda)^n_r$.

In words: every $r$-colouring of the $n$-subsets of a set of size $\kappa$ has a homogeneous set of size $\lambda$. Finite Ramsey's theorem (see [[ramsey]]) says that for every $k$ there is a finite $N$ with $N \to (k)^2_2$; the least such $N$ is $R(k)$.

blocks.title: Infinite Ramsey theorem (Ramsey, 1930)
blocks.body:
For all positive integers $n$ and $r$,
$$\aleph_0 \to (\aleph_0)^n_r.$$
That is, for every colouring of the $n$-element subsets of $\mathbb N$ with $r$ colours there is an infinite $H \subseteq \mathbb N$ all of whose $n$-element subsets have the same colour.

Induction on $n$. For $n = 1$ this is the infinite [[pigeonhole]] principle: if $\mathbb N$ is split into $r$ classes, one class is infinite.

Assume the statement for $n - 1$ and let $c$ colour $[\mathbb N]^n$ with $r$ colours. We build elements $a_0 < a_1 < a_2 < \cdots$, infinite sets $\mathbb N = X_0 \supseteq X_1 \supseteq X_2 \supseteq \cdots$ and colours $c_0, c_1, c_2, \ldots$ as follows. Given the infinite set $X_i$, let $a_i = \min X_i$. Colour each $(n-1)$-subset $s$ of $X_i \setminus \{a_i\}$ with the colour $c(\{a_i\} \cup s)$. By the induction hypothesis there is an infinite $X_{i+1} \subseteq X_i \setminus \{a_i\}$ on whose $(n-1)$-subsets this colouring is constant, say equal to $c_i$.

Every later element $a_j$ ($j > i$) lies in $X_{i+1}$. So any $n$-set of the form $\{a_i\} \cup s$ with $s \subseteq \{a_{i+1}, a_{i+2}, \ldots\}$ has colour $c_i$; in other words, the colour of an $n$-subset of $\{a_0, a_1, \ldots\}$ depends only on its smallest element. By the case $n = 1$, infinitely many indices $i$ share the same colour $c_i$, say all $i \in I$. Then $H = \{a_i : i \in I\}$ is infinite, and every $n$-subset of $H$ has colour $c_i$ for its least element $a_i$, which is the common colour. So $H$ is homogeneous.

blocks.title: From infinite to finite: compactness
blocks.body:
The infinite theorem implies the finite one without any estimates, by a compactness argument (second example). This kind of argument, related to compactness in topology (see [[compactness]]) and to König's lemma on infinite trees, gives no bound on $R(k)$, only its existence.

Compactness can prove more than it seems. Paris and Harrington found in 1977 a slight strengthening of finite Ramsey's theorem: one also asks that the homogeneous set $H$ have at least $\min H$ elements. This statement is true, and it follows from the infinite Ramsey theorem by compactness, but it cannot be proved in Peano arithmetic. It was the first natural example of a true statement about finite sets that is independent of Peano arithmetic.

blocks.title: Uncountable sets: where the analogy fails
blocks.body: One might hope that $\kappa \to (\kappa)^2_2$ for every infinite cardinal $\kappa$, or at least that $2^{\aleph_0} \to (\aleph_1)^2_2$: every 2-colouring of the pairs of real numbers has an uncountable homogeneous set. Sierpiński showed that this fails.

Using the axiom of choice, well-order the real numbers: fix a well-ordering $\prec$ of $\mathbb R$. Colour a pair $\{x, y\}$ with $x \prec y$ red if $x < y$ and blue if $x > y$. So a pair is red when the well-ordering and the usual order agree on it.

Suppose $H \subseteq \mathbb R$ is homogeneous of size $\aleph_1$. The well-ordering $\prec$ restricted to $H$ is a well-ordering of an uncountable set, so it has an initial segment of order type $\omega_1$: elements $y_\xi$, indexed by the countable ordinals $\xi$, with $y_\xi \prec y_\eta$ whenever $\xi < \eta$.

If $H$ is red, then $y_\xi < y_\eta$ whenever $\xi < \eta$: the $y_\xi$ form a strictly increasing sequence of real numbers of length $\omega_1$. For each $\xi$ choose a rational number $q_\xi$ with $y_\xi < q_\xi < y_{\xi+1}$. The open intervals $(y_\xi, y_{\xi+1})$ are pairwise disjoint, so the $q_\xi$ are distinct, and we get an injection from the uncountable set $\omega_1$ into the countable set $\mathbb Q$, which is impossible. If $H$ is blue, the same argument applies to the strictly decreasing sequence. Hence no homogeneous set of size $\aleph_1$ exists.

blocks.title: Positive results and independence
blocks.body:
The positive counterpart is the Erdős–Rado theorem (1956): for every infinite cardinal $\kappa$,
$$(2^\kappa)^+ \to (\kappa^+)^2_\kappa .$$
For $\kappa = \aleph_0$ it says that the pairs of a set of size $(2^{\aleph_0})^+$, coloured with countably many colours, have a homogeneous set of size $\aleph_1$. Sierpiński's theorem shows that $(2^{\aleph_0})^+$ cannot be replaced by $2^{\aleph_0}$ even for two colours, so this is sharp. We do not prove Erdős–Rado here; the proof is a transfinite refinement of the least-element construction used for the infinite Ramsey theorem.

These two results already produce a statement that ZFC cannot decide:
$$\aleph_2 \to (\aleph_1)^2_2 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \text{CH}.$$
If CH holds, then $(2^{\aleph_0})^+ = \aleph_2$, and Erdős–Rado gives $\aleph_2 \to (\aleph_1)^2_2$. If CH fails, then $2^{\aleph_0} \ge \aleph_2$, so there is a set of $\aleph_2$ real numbers, and Sierpiński's colouring restricted to it has no homogeneous set of size $\aleph_1$ (the proof above works for any set of reals). Since CH is independent of ZFC, so is $\aleph_2 \to (\aleph_1)^2_2$.

At the other extreme, an uncountable cardinal $\kappa$ with $\kappa \to (\kappa)^2_2$ is called weakly compact. Such cardinals are inaccessible, and ZFC cannot prove that they exist (if ZFC is consistent). So the simplest-looking uncountable analogue of Ramsey's theorem is a large cardinal axiom.

Exponent $\omega$ behaves differently again. One can ask for a 2-colouring of the infinite subsets of $\mathbb N$ with an infinite homogeneous set. With the axiom of choice there are colourings with none (fourth example). For colourings that are definable in a simple way, however, homogeneous sets do exist: Galvin and Prikry proved in 1973 that every Borel colouring has one.

blocks.title: Monotone subsequences
blocks.body: Prove that every sequence $x_1, x_2, \ldots$ of real numbers has an infinite subsequence that is strictly increasing, constant, or strictly decreasing.
blocks.solution:
Colour each pair $\{i, j\}$ with $i < j$ by one of three colours, according to whether $x_i < x_j$, $x_i = x_j$ or $x_i > x_j$. By $\aleph_0 \to (\aleph_0)^2_3$ there is an infinite set $H$ of indices on which the colouring is constant. Listing $H$ in increasing order $i_1 < i_2 < \cdots$, the subsequence $x_{i_1}, x_{i_2}, \ldots$ is strictly increasing, constant or strictly decreasing according to the colour. (Each consecutive pair has the common colour, and so does every pair.)

The finite analogue is the Erdős–Szekeres theorem: any $n^2 + 1$ distinct reals in sequence contain a monotone subsequence of length $n + 1$, and $n^2$ do not suffice.

blocks.title: Finite Ramsey from infinite Ramsey
blocks.body: Deduce from $\aleph_0 \to (\aleph_0)^2_2$, without any estimates, that for every $k$ there is a finite $N$ with $N \to (k)^2_2$.
blocks.solution:
Suppose not: for some $k$ and every $N$ there is a colouring $c_N$ of the pairs of $\{1, \dots, N\}$ with no homogeneous $k$-set. List all pairs of positive integers as $p_1, p_2, p_3, \ldots$.

We build a colouring $c$ of all pairs of $\mathbb N$. Let $S_0$ be the set of all $N$. Infinitely many $N \in S_0$ have $p_1 \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}$, and among them infinitely many give $p_1$ the same colour; call that colour $c(p_1)$ and the infinite set of such $N$ $S_1$. Repeat: from the infinite set $S_{j-1}$, keep those $N$ with $p_j \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}$ (all but finitely many); among them some colour is taken by $c_N(p_j)$ for infinitely many $N$. Call that colour $c(p_j)$ and let $S_j$ be the infinite set of those $N$. By construction, every $N \in S_j$ agrees with $c$ on $p_1, \dots, p_j$.

By the infinite Ramsey theorem, $c$ has an infinite homogeneous set; take $k$ of its elements, forming a set $K$. The pairs inside $K$ are among $p_1, \dots, p_J$ for some $J$. Any $N \in S_J$ is defined on these pairs and agrees with $c$ there, so $K$ is a homogeneous $k$-set for $c_N$, a contradiction.

blocks.title: Infinite point sets
blocks.body: Show that every infinite set of points in the plane contains an infinite subset that either lies on a single line or has no three points on a line.
blocks.solution:
Take a countably infinite subset $X$. Colour each 3-element subset of $X$ red if its points are collinear and blue otherwise. By $\aleph_0 \to (\aleph_0)^3_2$ there is an infinite homogeneous $H \subseteq X$.

If $H$ is blue, no three of its points are collinear. If $H$ is red, fix two points $a, b \in H$; every other $c \in H$ is collinear with $a$ and $b$, so lies on the line $ab$, and all of $H$ is on that line.

blocks.title: No Ramsey theorem for infinite exponent
blocks.body: Using the axiom of choice, construct a 2-colouring of the infinite subsets of $\mathbb N$ such that no infinite $H \subseteq \mathbb N$ has all its infinite subsets of the same colour.
blocks.solution:
Call infinite sets $X, Y \subseteq \mathbb N$ equivalent if their symmetric difference $X \triangle Y$ is finite. This is an equivalence relation. By the axiom of choice, pick one representative $r(X)$ from each equivalence class, so that $r(X) = r(Y)$ whenever $X$ and $Y$ are equivalent. Colour $X$ red if $|X \triangle r(X)|$ is even and blue if it is odd.

Let $H$ be any infinite set, $m = \min H$ and $H' = H \setminus \{m\}$. Both are infinite subsets of $H$, and they are equivalent, so $r(H') = r(H) =: r$. Since $H' \triangle r = (H \triangle r) \triangle \{m\}$, the sizes $|H' \triangle r|$ and $|H \triangle r|$ differ by exactly one. So $H$ and $H'$ have different colours, and $H$ is not homogeneous.

blocks.body:
- Homogeneous means every $n$-subset of $H$ has the same colour, not merely the $n$-subsets of consecutive elements. In the proof above, the reduction to the least element is what makes the colour depend on one index only.
- The arrow relation is monotone: if $\kappa \to (\lambda)^n_r$, then it remains true when $\kappa$ is increased or $\lambda$ or $r$ is decreased. Decreasing $n$ is also allowed when $\lambda$ is infinite (see the exercises), but not in general when $\lambda$ is finite: $3 \to (3)^3_2$ holds trivially, while $3 \not\to (3)^2_2$. Negative relations go the other way.
- The uncountable analogue of the infinite Ramsey theorem fails in ZFC for $2^{\aleph_0}$ (Sierpiński), and its validity for $\aleph_2$ depends on CH. Do not transfer the countable proof naively: a transfinite version of the construction must pass through limit stages, where the intersection of the nested sets $X_i$ built so far can be empty. Controlling this is exactly what costs the jump from $2^{\aleph_0}$ to $(2^{\aleph_0})^+$ in the Erdős–Rado theorem.
- Compactness arguments prove that finite numbers exist without bounding them. The Paris–Harrington theorem shows that this loss can be essential.
- Counterexamples like the one for exponent $\omega$ use the axiom of choice in an essential way; by the Galvin–Prikry theorem, no Borel colouring can be one.

- [[ramsey]]: finite Ramsey theory, which compactness derives from the infinite theorem.
- [[ramsey-arithmetic]]: Hindman's theorem (1974), that every finite colouring of $\mathbb N$ has an infinite set all of whose finite sums have one colour, is an infinite Ramsey theorem with a slick proof via ultrafilters.
- [[compactness]]: the passage from infinite to finite statements is a topological compactness argument in disguise (Tychonoff's theorem for the space of colourings).
- [[hypergraphs]]: colouring $n$-subsets is colouring the edges of a complete $n$-uniform hypergraph.
- [[real-numbers]]: Sierpiński's argument rests on the countable dense subset $\mathbb Q$ of $\mathbb R$.

checks.python:
import random
random.seed(9)
for _ in range(2000):
    H=set(random.sample(range(60),random.randint(1,30))); r=set(random.sample(range(60),random.randint(0,30)))
    m=min(H); H2=H-{m}
    assert abs(len(H2^r)-len(H^r))==1
    assert (H2^r)==((H^r)^{m})

from itertools import combinations, product
def arrow(N,lam,n,r):
    S=list(combinations(range(N),n))
    for col in product(range(r),repeat=len(S)):
        c=dict(zip(S,col))
        if not any(len({c[s] for s in combinations(H,n)})==1 for H in combinations(range(N),lam)): return False
    return True
